title: Psalm 85: Revive Us Again
summary: The psalm remembers a time when God showed favor to his land, restored Jacob, and forgave his people's sin. Yet the people are in trouble again, and they ask God to turn from his anger and revive them. A voice then listens for God's answer and hears a promise of peace: steadfast love and faithfulness meet, righteousness and peace kiss, and the land yields its harvest.
story: Psalm 85 is the second of the Korahite psalms that gather near the end of Book III (Psalms 84 to 88). Book III is the Psalter's book of crisis, moving through the destroyed sanctuary of Psalm 74 and the pleas of Psalms 79 and 80 toward the lament over David's fallen throne in Psalm 89. Psalm 85 names a particular kind of distress: the ache of living after a great deliverance that has not turned out as hoped. God has already forgiven and restored, and still the people need restoring. The psalm doesn't resolve that tension by pretending all is well; it waits for God to speak and hears him promise a future in which his glory dwells in the land. That hope reaches forward past the Psalter to the prophets' visions of full restoration.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to the sons of Korah, a family of Levitical temple singers. As with all the headings, scholars debate whether it records authorship or marks the collection the psalm came from.

The key phrase for dating is in verse 1: "You restored Jacob from captivity". Many interpreters read it as a reference to the return of Jewish exiles from Babylon after Cyrus of Persia conquered Babylon in 539 BC and permitted them to go home (Ezra 1). On that reading, the psalm fits the difficult decades that followed, when the returned community faced crop failure, poverty, and opposition, and the rebuilt temple seemed a shadow of the old one (Haggai 1:6-11; Ezra 3:12). The prayer for the land to yield its increase fits that setting well. Other scholars note that the Hebrew idiom behind "restored from captivity" can also mean more generally to restore someone's fortunes (it is used of Job in Job 42:10), and they place the psalm earlier, after some other national calamity such as a drought or military defeat. The psalm doesn't name its occasion, and its language has let later generations pray it for many different restorations.
cultural:
For an ancient Israelite, the condition of the land was a direct sign of the state of the covenant. Deuteronomy promised rain and harvest to a people who kept faith with God and warned of drought and failed crops when they did not (Deuteronomy 28:1-24). So when the psalm moves from forgiveness of sin in verse 2 to the land yielding its increase in verse 12, a first reader would not have seen two separate subjects. Sin, divine anger, barren fields, and restored harvests all belonged to one relationship.

The psalm's language of covering sin (verse 2) draws on the vocabulary of the temple, where sacrifice dealt with sin before God. The idea of God's glory dwelling in the land (verse 9) recalls the cloud of glory that filled the tabernacle and Solomon's temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:10-11). Ezekiel had seen that glory leave the temple before Jerusalem fell (Ezekiel 10) and had been promised its return (Ezekiel 43:1-5). A community living after the exile would have longed to see that promise kept.
literary: The psalm is a communal lament with an unusual structure in three movements. Verses 1 to 3 look back, with a string of verbs in the past tense: God showed favor, restored, forgave, covered, withheld, and turned. Verses 4 to 7 turn to present need, repeating the verb turn or restore (shuv) in a new direction: the God who turned from his anger is asked to turn to his people again. Verses 8 to 13 are the answer, introduced by a single voice, perhaps a priest or temple prophet, who says "I will listen to what God the LORD will say". The answer is built on personified pairs. Loving devotion and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss; faithfulness sprouts up from the earth and righteousness looks down from heaven. The picture is of heaven and earth coming back into harmony, and it ends with righteousness walking ahead of God like a herald preparing his road.

outline.t: A plea: restore us and revive us again
Listening for God's word of peace
Love, faithfulness, righteousness, and peace meet

doctrines.note: The psalm uses the word salvation three times (verses 4, 7, and 9) and shows it as both a past gift and a future hope. Salvation includes forgiveness of sin, restoration of the people, and God's presence dwelling among them.

The promise of peace comes with a condition: God speaks peace to his people so that they will "not ... return to folly" (verse 8). Restoration is received by those who fear him and turn from the ways that brought his anger.
The psalm holds on to God's promises while conditions remain hard. It trusts that the God who acted before will act again and that his glory will dwell in the land.

words.note: Shuv, to return or turn. The verb runs through the psalm: God turned (restored) Jacob in verse 1, turned from his anger in verse 3, is asked to turn his people back in verse 4, and to revive them again (literally to turn and give life) in verse 6. The people, in turn, are not to return to folly in verse 8. The psalm's hope depends on God turning first.

Chesed, loving devotion. It names God's steadfast, loyal love within his covenant, a love that keeps faith with his people even when they have failed. In verse 10 it is paired with faithfulness, echoing God's self-description in Exodus 34:6.

Shalom, peace. The word is broader than the absence of conflict. It means wholeness, well-being, and right relationship with God, neighbor, and the land. In verse 10 peace kisses righteousness: true peace is never separated from what is right.

Tsedeq, righteousness. Rightness according to God's standard, including the justice that sets wrongs right. Here it appears three times, looking down from heaven and walking ahead of God to prepare his way.

christ: The psalm longs for a day when God's glory dwells in the land and when loving devotion and faithfulness, righteousness and peace, are no longer at odds. The New Testament announces that God's glory has come to dwell among his people in Jesus (John 1:14, where John says we beheld his glory, full of grace and truth). Christian readers have long seen in verse 10 a picture of the cross, where God's justice and his mercy meet rather than cancel each other, and where Paul says God shows himself both just and the one who justifies (Romans 3:25-26). That reading is a theological reflection on the psalm rather than a prediction in it, but it follows the psalm's own logic: forgiveness (verse 2) and righteousness (verse 13) belong together. The psalm's last line, righteousness going before God to prepare the way for his steps, echoes the prophetic call to prepare the LORD's way (Isaiah 40:3), which the Gospels apply to John the Baptist's preparation for Jesus.
questions: The psalm prays for a people who have already been restored and still need reviving. Where do you find yourself between a past work of God and a future you are still waiting for?
Verse 8 begins with listening: "I will listen to what God the LORD will say". What would it look like for your prayer to include more listening?
Righteousness and peace kiss in verse 10. Where have you seen people try to have peace without righteousness, or righteousness without peace?
